india-macro.title: 'Creditors can't seek claims beyond okayed resolution plan'
india-macro.summary: Creditors seeking duplicate recoveries from group companies after a resolution plan is finalized will be disappointed, the NCLT ruled. JM Financial ARC's bid to recover more from KSK Mahanadi Power via guarantees was dismissed, as the tribunal found their admitted dues were already fully satisfied. This landmark judgment clarifies that approved resolution plans are binding, preventing further claims outside their scope.
india-macro.quick_take: The NCLT ruled that creditors cannot pursue extra claims beyond what was decided in the approved resolution plan for KSK Mahanadi Power, confirming that such plans are final.
india-macro.simplified_article: The National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) ruled that creditors, like JM Financial ARC, cannot seek more money from KSK Mahanadi Power after a resolution plan has been finalized. This decision happened because JM Financial attempted to claim additional amounts using guarantees, but the tribunal found that their current claims were already paid off. Resolution plans are agreements that outline how debts will be repaid, and this ruling makes it clear that once approved, they are legally binding. Moving forward, creditors cannot try to recover more money than what is stated in these plans, which may affect similar cases involving other companies and creditors going forward.
india-macro.investor_impact: This ruling could lead to increased stability in the financial sector since it reinforces the finality of resolution plans, which means companies in similar situations will have clearer guidelines on how debts are managed. Investors in distressed companies, particularly in the power sector, may feel more secure knowing that existing agreements will be honored without extra claims complicating finances.

key_terms.meaning: A resolution plan is an agreement that outlines how a company will repay its debts; it's important because it sets clear expectations for all parties involved.

crypto.title: Private keys, not smart contracts, caused 40% of crypto's $16 billion hack losses. Here's whats being done.

crypto.quick_take: Private keys, not smart contracts, were responsible for 40% of the $16 billion losses from crypto hacks, highlighting a serious security issue that needs addressing.
crypto.simplified_article: A recent report revealed that 40% of the $16 billion lost in crypto hacks was due to problems with private keys, which are like digital passwords that secure access to cryptocurrencies. This issue has been largely overlooked while more focus was put on smart contracts, which are self-executing agreements in the crypto world. As the industry recognizes the importance of securing private keys, efforts are being made to improve this aspect, but they're not being implemented consistently across the board. Moving forward, crypto users and companies will need to invest more in protecting private keys to prevent future losses and enhance security.
crypto.investor_impact: For people holding cryptocurrencies, this news could mean increased security measures, which may involve additional costs for wallets or services that protect private keys. If companies address these vulnerabilities seriously, it may restore trust in the crypto market, potentially stabilizing prices and encouraging more investment.
